VEDAL: Variational Error-Driven Asynchronous Learning for 3D Gaussian Splatting Pruning

Aoduo Li Affiliation: Guangdong University of Technology    Jiancheng Li Affiliation: Guangdong University of Technology    Huan Ye Affiliation: Guangdong University of Technology    Hongjian Xu Affiliation: Guangdong University of Technology    Shiting Wu Affiliation: Huizhou Boluo Power Supply Bureau, Guangdong Power Grid Co., Ltd.    Xiujun Zhang Affiliation: Shenzhen Polytechnic University    Zimeng Li ††thanks: Corresponding authors. Affiliation: Shenzhen Polytechnic University    Xuhang Chen11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Huizhou University E-mail li_zimeng@szpu.edu.cn, xuhangc@hzu.edu.cn
Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves remarkable novel view synthesis quality with real-time rendering, yet suffers from excessive memory consumption due to millions of Gaussian primitives. Existing pruning methods rely on heuristic importance scores or synchronous batch updates, leading to suboptimal compression and training instability. We propose VEDAL, a variational framework that formulates Gaussian pruning through free-energy minimization. Our approach combines (1) a prediction-error gating mechanism that asynchronously activates pruning only after per-Gaussian importance estimates stabilize, and (2) a variational uncertainty head that models retention decisions as latent Bernoulli variables with a sparsity-inducing prior. The resulting objective balances reconstruction fidelity against model complexity and makes the pruning schedule depend on convergence rather than on a fixed global iteration count. Experiments on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks&Temples, and Deep Blending show that VEDAL achieves 5.2×5.2\times compression with only 0.310.31 dB PSNR drop and consistent, albeit modest, gains over the evaluated pruning baselines, while maintaining real-time rendering at 185185 FPS. The code is available at https://github.com/AsakaTigar/VEDAL.

Keywords: 
3D Gaussian Splatting Neural Rendering Model Pruning Variational Inference Scene Compression

1 Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [15] achieves real-time novel view synthesis via tile-based alpha-blending of anisotropic Gaussian primitives. However, adaptive densification produces millions of Gaussians (1–4 GB per scene), limiting deployment on memory-constrained devices. Many are redundant, motivating principled compression. This is particularly critical for 3D applications [19, 45, 18, 38, 25, 20, 21, 24, 48, 13]. More broadly, recent visual intelligence research has also expanded to multimodal reasoning evaluation, motivating models and representations that are not only accurate but also efficient and reliable [37].

Existing methods [7, 17, 8, 10, 28, 22, 27, 23, 26, 14] use heuristic importance scores and synchronous removal, ignoring that different Gaussians converge at vastly different rates. Primitives in textured regions stabilize quickly; those in specular or occluded areas need far more iterations. Unlike neural-network pruning [34, 29], where all weights see every sample, each Gaussian receives view-dependent gradients, creating heterogeneous convergence. We introduce convergence-conditional variational inference, activating the ELBO’s KL regularizer per-variable only after its reconstruction signal stabilizes. VEDAL comprises:

  1. 1.

    A prediction-error gate maintains per-Gaussian EMA estimates of leave-one-out importance and asynchronously activates pruning eligibility once each estimate converges (Section 3.3).

  2. 2.

    A variational uncertainty head models the retention decision for each eligible Gaussian as a Bernoulli latent variable and optimizes an ELBO with a sparsity-inducing KL prior (Section 3.4).

We derive a closed-form retention–error correspondence (Proposition 1): optimal retention is a sigmoid of the importance-to-KL-weight ratio, motivating convergence-aware gating. Experiments on Mip-NeRF 360 [1], Tanks&Temples [16], and Deep Blending [11] show 5.2×5.2\times compression with 0.310.31 dB PSNR drop and consistent improvements over the evaluated pruning baselines at 185 FPS.

Contributions: (1) Convergence-conditional variational inference for 3DGS pruning with a retention–error theorem; (2) an asynchronous prediction-error gate; (3) a variational uncertainty head for learned retention; (4) consistent compression–quality improvements over the evaluated baselines on three benchmarks.

2 Related Work

3D Gaussian Splatting.  3DGS [15] renders via anisotropic Gaussian primitives with spherical harmonics. Extensions address surface quality [12], anchors [31], anti-aliasing [47], dynamics [44, 46, 42], and language-driven scene editing [3]; yet, densification produces millions of primitives (∼236{\sim}236 B each), creating a memory bottleneck.

Pruning.  LightGaussian [7] ranks by significance; Compact3D [17] learns binary masks; Mini-Splatting [8] constrains count during densification; PUP 3D-GS [10] uses Hessian sensitivity; MaskGaussian [28] learns probabilistic masks—closest to our Bernoulli posteriors but without convergence-aware gating. More recent work broadens the landscape. SVR-GS [39] introduces spatially variant regularisation for probabilistic masks, Gradient-Driven Natural Selection [6] uses opacity regularisation as a learnable survival signal, and Clean-GS [33] removes floaters using sparse semantic masks. These methods reinforce the importance of non-uniform sparsity, but they do not explicitly address when the pruning signal of each Gaussian becomes reliable enough to activate variational pressure. Our focus is therefore complementary: we keep the pruning decision learnable while conditioning it on convergence.

Attribute compression.  Quantization [35, 5, 9], structural [31, 36], training-free codebook methods such as FlexGaussian [41], and optimization-free feedforward compression such as FCGS [4] reduce per-Gaussian storage rather than count; also, there are many other methods [50, 43, 49, 51]. These directions are largely orthogonal to pruning-based count reduction, which is why we study their combination with VEDAL in Section 4.5. Generative and editing-oriented efficiency methods [40, 30] are also complementary.

Variational pruning.  Variational Dropout [34] and Bayesian Compression [29] prune weights via ELBO, assuming i.i.d. gradients. In 3DGS, view-dependent gradients create heterogeneous convergence; our convergence-conditional extension activates KL per-variable only after its signal stabilises (Proposition 1).

3 Method

3.1 Preliminaries

3DGS [15] models a scene as NN anisotropic Gaussians {Gi}i=1N\{G_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}, each with position 𝝁i∈ℝ3\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{3}, covariance 𝚺i=Ri​Si​Si⊤​Ri⊤\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i}\!=\!R_{i}S_{i}S_{i}^{\top}R_{i}^{\top} (rotation RiR_{i}, diagonal scale Si=diag⁡(si,1,si,2,si,3)S_{i}\!=\!\mathrm{diag}(s_{i,1},s_{i,2},s_{i,3})), opacity αi\alpha_{i}, and SH colour coefficients 𝐜i\mathbf{c}_{i}. Rendering uses depth-sorted alpha-blending: C⁡(𝐩)=∑i∈𝒩⁡(𝐩)ci​αi​∏j<i(1−αj)C(\mathbf{p})=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{p})}c_{i}\,\alpha_{i}\prod_{j<i}(1{-}\alpha_{j}). Training minimises ℒrecon=(1−λ)​ℒ1+λ​ℒD-SSIM\mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}=(1{-}\lambda)\mathcal{L}_{1}+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{D-SSIM}}.

3.2 Convergence-Conditional Variational Inference

We introduce latent binary variables 𝐳={zi}i=1N\mathbf{z}=\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} (zi=1z_{i}{=}1: retain; zi=0z_{i}{=}0: prune). Given training images 𝒟\mathcal{D}, the marginal likelihood involves a combinatorial sum:

logp(𝒟|𝒢)=log∑𝐳p(𝒟|𝒢,𝐳)p(𝐳).\log p(\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{G})=\log\!\sum_{\mathbf{z}}p(\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{G},\mathbf{z})\,p(\mathbf{z}). (1)

We optimise the evidence lower bound (ELBO) [2]:

log⁡p⁡(𝒟|𝒢)≥𝔼qϕ​(𝐳)​[log⁡p⁡(𝒟|𝒢,𝐳)]⏟reconstruction−KL(qϕ(𝐳)∥p(𝐳))⏟complexity.\log p(\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{G})\;\geq\;\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z})}\!\bigl[\log p(\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{G},\mathbf{z})\bigr]}_{\text{reconstruction}}\;-\;\underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\!\bigl(q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z})\|p(\mathbf{z})\bigr)}_{\text{complexity}}. (2)

Factorised posterior.  qϕ​(𝐳)=∏i=1NBernoulli⁡(zi,πi)q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z})=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(z_{i};\pi_{i}), where πi=σ⁡(fϕ​(Gi))\pi_{i}=\sigma(f_{\phi}(G_{i})) is produced by the variational head (Section 3.4) for all NN Gaussians.

Sparsity prior.  p⁡(𝐳)=∏i=1NBernoulli⁡(zi,ρ)p(\mathbf{z})=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(z_{i};\rho) with ρ<0.5\rho{<}0.5, yielding per-Gaussian KL:

Di=πi​log⁡πiρ+(1−πi)​log⁡1−πi1−ρ.D_{i}\;=\;\pi_{i}\log\frac{\pi_{i}}{\rho}+(1{-}\pi_{i})\log\frac{1{-}\pi_{i}}{1{-}\rho}. (3)

Convergence conditioning.  Standard variational pruning applies KL to all variables simultaneously, but in 3DGS each Gaussian’s importance is reliable only after sufficient view coverage. We condition KL activation on a convergence predicate gi(t)∈{0,1}g_{i}^{(t)}\!\in\!\{0,1\} (Section 3.3):

ℒKL(t)=1|𝒜(t)|∑i:gi(t)=1Di,𝒜(t)={i:gi(t)=1}.\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}^{(t)}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}^{(t)}|}\sum_{i:\,g_{i}^{(t)}=1}D_{i},\qquad\mathcal{A}^{(t)}=\{i:g_{i}^{(t)}{=}1\}. (4)

Retention–error correspondence. 

Proposition 1

Let δi=ℒrecon​(𝒢∖Gi)−ℒrecon​(𝒢)\delta_{i}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}(\mathcal{G}{\setminus}G_{i})-\mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}(\mathcal{G}). Under the gated ELBO with KL weight λKL\lambda_{\text{KL}} and prior ρ\rho, the optimal retention probability satisfies πi∗=σ⁡(δi/λKL+log⁡(ρ/(1−ρ)))\pi_{i}^{*}=\sigma\!\bigl(\delta_{i}/\lambda_{\text{KL}}+\log(\rho/(1{-}\rho))\bigr).

Proof sketch. Differentiating the per-Gaussian negative ELBO Fi​(πi)F_{i}(\pi_{i}) and solving ∂Fi/∂πi=0\partial F_{i}/\partial\pi_{i}{=}0 (convex in πi\pi_{i}) yields the sigmoid form. Full proof in supplementary.

This sigmoid reveals that when δi\delta_{i} is noisy (pre-convergence), retention oscillates. Activating KL only after δi\delta_{i} converges ensures stable decisions, motivating the gate below.

Coupling assumption.  Proposition 1 treats Fi​(πi)F_{i}(\pi_{i}) as independent, ignoring transmittance coupling. We systematically quantify this across 20 random k=50k{=}50 neighbourhoods per scene. The additive ∑δi\sum\delta_{i} overestimates true loss by 7.8±2.1%7.8{\pm}2.1\% (Lego), 9.2±2.8%9.2{\pm}2.8\% (Garden, higher depth complexity), and 6.5±1.9%6.5{\pm}1.9\% (Chair, sparse). Overestimation correlates with mean opacity overlap (r=0.74r{=}0.74); worst case is 14%14\% in dense specular clusters. These measurements indicate that the additive approximation is conservative rather than exact. We therefore interpret Proposition 1 as a first-order analysis of pruning pressure, not as a claim of exact Gaussian independence. In practice, the overestimation shifts the gate toward delaying pruning instead of accelerating it, which is consistent with the low gate-reversal and co-pruning rates reported in Section 4.5.

3.3 Prediction-Error Gate

For each GiG_{i}, we maintain an EMA of its leave-one-out importance:

e¯i(t)=β​e¯i(t−1)+(1−β)​ei(t),β=0.99,\bar{e}_{i}^{(t)}=\beta\,\bar{e}_{i}^{(t-1)}+(1{-}\beta)\,e_{i}^{(t)},\qquad\beta=0.99, (5)

where ei(t)e_{i}^{(t)} is the per-pixel ℒ1+λ​ℒD-SSIM\mathcal{L}_{1}{+}\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\text{D-SSIM}} change when GiG_{i}’s opacity is set to zero in the cached tile buffer (SH colours frozen, evaluated over all pixels covered by GiG_{i}’s projected footprint).

Efficient approximation.  Exact leave-one-out requires O⁡(N)O(N) renders. We cache ci​αi​Tic_{i}\alpha_{i}T_{i} (Ti=∏j<i(1−αj)T_{i}{=}\prod_{j<i}(1{-}\alpha_{j})) from the tile rasteriser and use a first-order approximation (ignoring downstream transmittance correction), refreshed every Δe=100\Delta_{e}{=}100 iterations at ≤3%{\leq}3\% overhead. Table 4 (right) validates this approximation across scenes and training stages: Spearman rs≥0.91r_{s}{\geq}0.91 at all checkpoints, with gate-decision agreement ≥96%{\geq}96\%; replacing the approximation with exact leave-one-out changes final PSNR by <0.03{<}0.03 dB.

Gating.  The adaptive threshold τ(t)=Percentilep​({e¯i(t)})\tau^{(t)}=\mathrm{Percentile}_{p}(\{\bar{e}_{i}^{(t)}\}) with p=0.3p{=}0.3 caps the eligible fraction. The gate gi(t)=𝟙[e¯i(t)<τ(t)]⋅𝟙[t>twarmup]g_{i}^{(t)}=\mathbb{1}[\bar{e}_{i}^{(t)}<\tau^{(t)}]\cdot\mathbb{1}[t>t_{\text{warmup}}] (twarmup=3000t_{\text{warmup}}{=}3000) activates asynchronously: easy-region Gaussians become eligible early; specular/occluded ones stay protected. Eligible fractions (5K→\to25K): Lego 12→31%12{\to}31\%, Garden 9→28%9{\to}28\%, Bicycle 7→26%7{\to}26\%, Kitchen 11→30%11{\to}30\%; gate reversal (a Gaussian crossing τ\tau back above after dropping below) is <2%{<}2\% in all cases. The gate is most conservative for highly translucent Gaussians (αi<0.1\alpha_{i}{<}0.1), which have noisy eie_{i} and rarely become eligible before 15K; for extreme specularities the EMA stabilises around 20K. The consistent pattern confirms defaults (p=0.3p{=}0.3, twarmup=3000t_{\text{warmup}}{=}3000) generalise without per-scene tuning.

3.4 Variational Uncertainty Head

A lightweight MLP computes the retention probability for every Gaussian:

πi=σ⁡(MLPϕ​([𝝁i,𝐬i,αi,e¯i])),𝐬i=diag⁡(Si)∈ℝ3,\pi_{i}=\sigma\!\bigl(\mathrm{MLP}_{\phi}([\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i},\mathbf{s}_{i},\alpha_{i},\bar{e}_{i}])\bigr),\quad\mathbf{s}_{i}=\mathrm{diag}(S_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, (6)

with two hidden layers (64 units, ReLU; ∼5{\sim}5K parameters). The head is evaluated for all NN Gaussians regardless of gate status, ensuring ℒsparse\mathcal{L}_{\text{sparse}} gradients flow to ungated Gaussians (Section 3.5) and pre-conditioning them before their gate activates.

Relaxation and masking.  We use Binary Concrete [32]: z~i=σ⁡((log⁡πi−log⁡(1−πi)+g1−g2)/τgs)\tilde{z}_{i}=\sigma\bigl((\log\pi_{i}-\log(1{-}\pi_{i})+g_{1}-g_{2})/\tau_{\text{gs}}\bigr) with τgs\tau_{\text{gs}} annealed 1.0→0.11.0{\to}0.1. We chose Binary Concrete over STE (biased gradient mismatch: −0.13-0.13 dB on Lego) and REINFORCE (high variance: −0.07-0.07 dB at 1.4×1.4\times training time). Masked opacity: α~i=αi​z~i\tilde{\alpha}_{i}=\alpha_{i}\tilde{z}_{i} if gi=1g_{i}{=}1 (gated), αi\alpha_{i} otherwise. At inference, zi=𝟙[πi>0.5]z_{i}=\mathbb{1}[\pi_{i}{>}0.5]. The position-aware MLP learns spatially smooth πi\pi_{i}, preventing catastrophic co-pruning of adjacent Gaussians (<1.2%{<}1.2\% of k=5k{=}5 NN clusters fully pruned; <0.5%{<}0.5\% at k=10k{=}10; Section 4.5).

3.5 Training Objective

ℒtotal=ℒrecon+λKL​ℒKL+λsparse​ℒsparse,\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}+\lambda_{\text{KL}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}+\lambda_{\text{sparse}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{sparse}}, (7)

where ℒrecon=(1−λ)​ℒ1+λ​ℒD-SSIM\mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}=(1{-}\lambda)\mathcal{L}_{1}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\text{D-SSIM}} uses masked opacities α~i\tilde{\alpha}_{i}, ℒKL\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}} is the convergence-conditioned KL (Eq. 4), and ℒsparse=1N​∑iπi\mathcal{L}_{\text{sparse}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\pi_{i} provides mild global sparsity pressure.

ℒKL\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}} applies only to gated Gaussians, whereas ℒsparse\mathcal{L}_{\text{sparse}} (λsparse=0.001\lambda_{\text{sparse}}{=}0.001) applies to all Gaussians throughout training. The two regularizers play different roles: the gated KL term controls how strongly already-eligible Gaussians are pushed toward the sparse prior, whereas ℒsparse\mathcal{L}_{\text{sparse}} provides a weak global signal before eligibility and helps stabilize ungated probabilities. Defaults: λKL=0.01\lambda_{\text{KL}}{=}0.01, ρ=0.3\rho{=}0.3, β=0.99\beta{=}0.99, twarmup=3000t_{\text{warmup}}{=}3000. Training: 7K 3DGS init ++ 23K fine-tuning (densification off); post-training, remove πi<0.5\pi_{i}{<}0.5.

4 Experiments

4.1 Setup

Datasets and Metrics.  Mip-NeRF 360 [1], Tanks&Temples [16], and Deep Blending [11]. Metrics: PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, compression ratio, FPS, and size. Baselines include LightGaussian [7], Compact3D [17], Mini-Splatting [8], PUP 3D-GS [10], and MaskGaussian [28] under a unified protocol. We discuss recent methods (SVR-GS, Clean-GS, etc.) in Section 2 as contextual baselines.

4.2 Main Results

Table 1 shows that VEDAL reaches 5.2×5.2\times compression with 0.310.31 dB PSNR drop. The margin over PUP 3D-GS (+0.05+0.05 dB) and MaskGaussian (+0.02+0.02 dB) is consistent across all datasets and is accompanied by the smallest model size. Perceptual gains match the sharper edge preservation in Fig. 3.

4.3 Ablation Study

Table 3 clarifies component roles. The KL term supplies compression pressure, but gating determines when it is safe to apply. Removing gating drops PSNR by 0.260.26 dB. Our EMA approximation validates against exact leave-one-out with Spearman rs≥0.91r_{s}{\geq}0.91.

4.4 Qualitative Analysis

Visual results in Fig. 3 and error maps in Fig. 4 show that VEDAL concentrates residual error on fine edges rather than on broad structures. This matches the sharper texture preservation seen in high-frequency regions like the Lego brick seams and drum hardware.

4.5 Secondary Analysis

Table 4 summarizes the secondary diagnostics. Panel (a) shows that λKL\lambda_{\text{KL}} is the primary rate–distortion knob, while panel (b) confirms that the leave-one-out approximation remains reliable across training stages. Combining VEDAL with attribute compression [41] yields 27.2×27.2\times total compression. Training overhead is modest (+12%+12\%), so the better compression regime is not paid for by a large optimization overhead.

4.6 Discussion

Pareto curves (Fig. 5(a)) show that VEDAL lies on a favorable frontier across reproduced sweeps rather than at a single cherry-picked operating point. Heterogeneous convergence (Fig. 5(c)) justifies our asynchronous mechanism: textured Gaussians settle early, while specular ones require more iterations. Learned probabilities (Fig. 5(d)) are spatially heterogeneous, preventing catastrophic co-pruning. The right block of Table 4 confirms that our O⁡(1)O(1) importance approximation remains accurate throughout training.

5 Conclusion

We presented VEDAL, a convergence-conditional variational framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting pruning. By introducing a prediction-error gate that asynchronously activates pruning pressure based on per-primitive reconstruction stability, we avoid the premature removal of Gaussians in complex regions that converge slowly. Our variational uncertainty head learns spatially smooth retention decisions that balance reconstruction fidelity against model complexity.

Experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate that VEDAL consistently improves the compression–quality trade-off over existing heuristic and synchronous pruning methods, achieving 5.2×5.2\times reduction in primitive count with minimal PSNR loss. The modular design of our framework allows it to be combined with orthogonal attribute compression techniques, reaching over 27×27\times total compression. Future work includes extending the convergence-aware gating mechanism to dynamic scene decomposition and exploring more sophisticated priors for structured sparsity.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
